title: Mumo Matemu v Trusted Society of Human Rights Alliance & 5 others

summary.facts: The appellant challenged clearance and appointment processes before the High Court via public interest petition. Respondents raised locus standi and procedural objections.
issues: Standing in public interest petitions under Article 22
Role of the courts in reviewing appointments to commissions
Whether the petition disclosed a cause of action
summary.holding: Public interest standing under Article 22 is broad; technical objections cannot defeat constitutional litigation where rights or public interest are engaged.
summary.ratio: Article 22 and the Fair Administrative Action Act require courts to resolve disputes on substance; standing rules must not become barriers to constitutional enforcement.
summary.obiter: The court emphasised that access to justice under Article 48 must be given real effect.

full_text: Court of Appeal decision on locus standi and public interest litigation under the Constitution of Kenya 2010. The Court held that the broad standing provisions in Article 22 enable persons acting in the public interest to institute constitutional claims. Procedural technicalities must not defeat substantive justice. Judicial review of administrative appointments requires engagement with merits where constitutional standards are implicated.

title: Mitu-Bell Welfare Society v Attorney General & 2 others

summary.facts: Residents of Mitu-Bell informal settlement faced eviction without adequate notice, consultation, or alternative settlement.
issues: Whether forced eviction without process violates Articles 40, 43 and 47
Duties of state agencies before evictions
Remedies available to affected communities
summary.holding: Evictions must comply with constitutional and human-rights standards including notice, consultation, and, where appropriate, resettlement.
summary.ratio: The right to accessible and adequate housing and fair administrative action constrains eviction powers; arbitrary demolitions are unconstitutional.
summary.obiter: Courts can issue structural remedies requiring plans for affected persons.

full_text: The High Court held that evictions from informal settlements must respect constitutional rights. State agencies must act lawfully, give notice, and consider alternatives. The decision is a leading Kenyan authority on socio-economic rights and forced evictions.

title: Njoya & 6 others v Attorney General & 4 others

summary.facts: Petitioners challenged the Constitution of Kenya Review Act and processes used to adopt a draft constitution.
issues: Whether Parliament could prescribe a process inconsistent with popular initiative requirements
Role of a referendum in constitutional replacement
summary.holding: Constitutional amendment and review processes must follow the supreme law; Parliament cannot rewrite constitutional rules by ordinary statute.
summary.ratio: The people are the source of constituent power; procedures for constitutional change must be constitutionally compliant.
summary.obiter: The court discussed the distinction between amendment and replacement of a constitution.

full_text: Leading pre-2010 authority on constitutional review. The High Court emphasised that constituent power belongs to the people and that statutory processes for constitutional review cannot override constitutional requirements.

title: Republic v Daniel Toroitich arap Moi & 2 others ex parte Gicheru

summary.facts: Applicant sought to reopen issues said to have been determined in prior proceedings involving land and public officers.
issues: Application of res judicata
Limitation periods for land claims
summary.holding: Matters already adjudicated between the same parties cannot be relitigated; limitation statutes apply.
summary.ratio: Finality of litigation and limitation statutes protect legal certainty.
summary.obiter: Public interest does not automatically open closed proceedings.

full_text: Illustrates Kenyan application of res judicata and the Limitation of Actions Act to claims involving public land and former state officers.

title: Judicial Service Commission v Speaker of the National Assembly & another

summary.facts: Dispute over interference with the independence of the Judiciary and the Judicial Service Commission.
issues: Scope of judicial independence under Articles 160–161
Whether other arms of government may direct the Judiciary
summary.holding: The Judiciary is subject only to the Constitution and the law; political organs cannot control judicial functions.
summary.ratio: Independence of the Judiciary is a constitutional guarantee essential to the rule of law.
summary.obiter: Institutional autonomy includes control of administrative decisions within the JSC.

full_text: Supreme Court authority reaffirming judicial independence. The Court held that executive and legislative organs may not direct or control the Judiciary or the JSC in the performance of their functions.

title: Centre for Rights Education and Awareness (CREAW) & another v Speaker of the National Assembly

summary.facts: Petitioners sought enforcement of the two-thirds gender principle in elective and appointive bodies.
issues: Whether Parliament had enacted legislation to implement the two-thirds gender rule
Consequences of legislative inaction
summary.holding: State organs have a duty to implement the Constitution; prolonged legislative inaction can be justiciable.
summary.ratio: Articles 27 and 81 require progressive realisation of gender equality in representation; courts may compel action.
summary.obiter: Structural orders may be used where systemic non-compliance is shown.

full_text: High Court decision on the two-thirds gender principle. The court found that failure to enact implementing legislation violated constitutional obligations on equality and representation.

title: Coalition for Reform and Democracy (CORD) & 2 others v Republic of Kenya & 10 others

summary.facts: Petitioners challenged provisions of the Security Laws (Amendment) Act 2014 alleged to limit fundamental freedoms.
issues: Whether security legislation disproportionately limited freedom of expression and media
Limitation analysis under Article 24
summary.holding: Several provisions were struck down as unconstitutional for failing the Article 24 limitation test.
summary.ratio: National security does not justify blanket limits on rights; each limitation must be necessary and proportionate.
summary.obiter: Counter-terrorism measures remain subject to the Bill of Rights.

full_text: Landmark constitutional review of security legislation. The High Court applied Article 24 and struck down provisions that unjustifiably restricted freedom of expression and other rights.

title: Kenya Commercial Bank Ltd & another v Samuel Kamau Macharia & 2 others

summary.facts: Dispute over bank's exercise of set-off and rights under security documents.
issues: Scope of contractual set-off
Whether bank acted within contractual and statutory powers
summary.holding: A bank may exercise contractual set-off where the contract clearly confers the right and conditions are met.
summary.ratio: Commercial contracts are enforced according to their terms subject to statutory controls on unconscionability.
summary.obiter: Courts will not rewrite commercial bargains absent vitiating factors.

full_text: Commercial law authority on bank set-off and enforcement of security. Illustrates contractual interpretation in Kenyan banking disputes.

title: Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission v National Super Alliance (NASA) & 3 others

summary.facts: Challenge to the 2017 presidential election results alleging irregularities and illegalities in transmission and tallying.
issues: Standard for nullification of a presidential election under Article 140(3)
Role of technology and results declaration forms
summary.holding: The presidential election of 8 August 2017 was declared invalid for non-compliance with the Constitution and the law.
summary.ratio: An election is a process, not an event; substantial compliance with electoral law is required, and systemic irregularities that affect integrity justify nullification.
summary.obiter: The Court ordered a fresh election within 60 days.

full_text: Historic Supreme Court decision annulling a presidential election in Africa. The Court held that IEBC failed to conduct the election in accordance with the Constitution and the Elections Act, and ordered a fresh poll.

title: Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission v Deepak Kamani & another

summary.facts: EACC sought recovery of assets alleged to be proceeds of crime connected to public procurement.
issues: Standard of proof in civil asset recovery
Meaning of unexplained assets
summary.holding: Civil recovery is determined on balance of probabilities; respondents must explain legitimate sources of wealth where prima facie case is shown.
summary.ratio: Anti-corruption civil processes are distinct from criminal prosecution and aim at recovery of public resources.
summary.obiter: Article 73 leadership and integrity values underpin recovery actions.

full_text: Illustrates civil asset recovery under anti-corruption legislation. Courts may order forfeiture where assets are shown to be proceeds of crime or unexplained wealth on the civil standard.

title: Kenya Ports Authority v Kenya Power & Lighting Company Limited

summary.facts: Dispute over wayleave and compensation for power lines across land used for port operations.
issues: Whether wayleaves require registration
Compensation for injurious affection
summary.holding: Statutory wayleaves must comply with land legislation; affected owners are entitled to compensation where rights are impaired.
summary.ratio: Private property rights under Article 40 require lawful acquisition of interests and fair compensation.
summary.obiter: Utilities must follow statutory procedures for wayleaves.

full_text: Environment and Land Court decision on wayleaves and compensation. Reinforces Article 40 protection of property and statutory compliance for infrastructure interests in land.

title: Thomas De La Rue v David Opondo Omutelema

summary.facts: Employee challenged termination on grounds of redundancy alleging lack of fair procedure and genuine operational need.
issues: Genuine redundancy requirements under Employment Act
Fair procedure and selection criteria
summary.holding: Redundancy must be genuine and conducted fairly, with notice and consultation; sham redundancy amounts to unfair termination.
summary.ratio: Section 40 Employment Act requires valid reason and fair process; courts examine substance over label.
summary.obiter: Compensation may include up to 12 months' wages.

full_text: Court of Appeal authority on redundancy. The employer must prove a genuine operational requirement and follow fair selection and notification procedures.
